A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MVU research, with matching authors, core framework and experiments. The main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original MVU and baseline evaluations on EgoSchema, NExT-QA, robotics datasets and Something-Something-v2, including component and inference ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds ActivityNet-QA results, controlled baseline comparisons and prompt-related experiments, including in its appendices.

M1.justification: V1 describes likelihood-ranking 16 frames to select eight and supplying the highest-ranked frame to MVU. V2 instead describes uniformly sampled frames, a center-frame input, and detection/tracking over 16 rather than eight frames. Appendix G also introduces free-form answer generation. These substantially revise input processing and inference, although Figure 3 and Appendix B retain inconsistent frame-selection references.

E1.justification: V2 adds ActivityNet-QA evaluation requiring open-ended answer generation, extending coverage beyond v1's answer selection and classification tasks. EgoSchema, NExT-QA, the existing robotics datasets and SSv2 remain; the SSv2 evaluation moves to Appendix H rather than being removed.

E2.justification: The detailed robotics comparison replaces SF-VLM with LLoVi, while retaining aggregate SF-VLM results in Table A.3. V2 adds naive likelihood selection and controlled frame-description comparators, plus ActivityNet-QA comparisons including Video-ChatGPT and VideoCoCa. Llama-2 and Gemma result rows disappear from the modality-constrained comparison. Main EgoSchema and NExT-QA comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Beyond revised frame sampling and detector frame counts, v2 introduces open-ended answer generation and matching following Maaz et al. (2023), and controlled frame-description experiments using eight, 16 and 180 frames. Existing principal dataset splits and zero-shot training conditions remain. These are reported protocol changes and additions; the PDFs do not establish which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds naive-versus-adapted likelihood selection and prompt sensitivity analyses, extends the selection ablation to NExT-QA, and tests object-centric information against frame descriptions under a shared final VLM. It also adds a robotics Just-LLM test. The frame-selection ablation disappears and modality combinations change in Table 5; the SSv2 motion ablation is retained unchanged in Table A.6.

E5.justification: Both versions report point accuracies and inference times without repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's prompt-sensitivity results do not introduce an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Reported MVU NExT-QA overall accuracy changes from 55.2% to 55.4%, and robotics aggregate accuracy from 25.0% to 30.4%. V2 adds ActivityNet-QA results of 42.2% for MVU versus 41.8% for LLoVi, and new control results. Modality-ablation entries change, and generation time changes from 8.65 to 12.7 seconds. These are revised or added results, not established same-setting improvements; main EgoSchema and SSv2 scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The likelihood factorization and cross-entropy selection derivation from v1 Section 3.2 are retained in v2 Appendix F.1. Object-set and trajectory definitions also remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem, proof or formal assumption is introduced.

C1.justification: V1 presents likelihood selection as a newly proposed central contribution and emphasizes its extension to frame selection. V2 instead claims adaptation of an existing selection technique and foregrounds modality-constrained evaluation. The central claim of training-free, object-centric language fusion remains, but the claimed methodological novelty is substantially narrowed.

C2.justification: V2 explains near-random robotics Just-LLM performance through limits of everyday world knowledge, attributes degradation with many frame descriptions to reduced signal-to-noise ratio, and discusses prompt sensitivity and possible domain-specific tuning. Appendix H also explicitly questions motion requirements of common video-QA benchmarks. V1's ethics discussion of inherited model biases is removed.

D1.justification: V2 adds answer-selection prompt pseudocode, describes heuristic prompt selection, and identifies the object tracker. Most backbone and hardware information is retained or relocated. V1's frame-selection prompt is removed, and its explicit code repository link and availability statement are replaced by a promise of future public release; actual repository availability cannot be determined from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Likelihood selection is repositioned from a proposed technique to an adaptation of established cloze prompting, explicitly attributed to Robinson et al. (2023). V2 also adds open-ended video-model references and robotics-related positioning, while removing individual robotics-dataset citations. The novelty reattribution is substantive, beyond the switch in citation style.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten. Modality-constrained variants move ahead of MVU, vision-tool explanations replace the frame-selection subsection, and likelihood derivations, experimental details and the SSv2 ablation move into reorganized appendices. Ethics, acknowledgements and author-contribution sections disappear.

P2.justification: V2 substantially reformats the document and reorganizes its displays: modality tables are condensed, ablation columns and rows change, new comparison tables appear, and the SSv2 table moves to the appendix. Captions and tables use new side-by-side arrangements. The four existing figures are largely reused and resized rather than replaced with new visual evidence.

improvement.justification: V2 improves scientific assessment through clearer attribution of likelihood selection, controlled frame-description and prompt comparisons, and explicit discussion of prompt sensitivity and domain limitations. Open-ended evaluation also supports broader applicability. These gains are tempered by conflicting frame-selection descriptions and removal of the concrete code-access link. The new controls and qualifications support a modest net improvement, rather than one inferred from higher reported scores.
